paragraphs: The paper asks how much detail a decoder needs about relationships among neurons to recover information from their activity. It constructs a hierarchy of simplified response models using maximum entropy. Each model retains correlations only up to a chosen order, making it possible to systematically compare more detailed descriptions with simpler ones.

The central step is to measure the information recovered when decoding uses one of these simplified models. Such a decoder is mismatched because its assumed response distribution differs from the fuller description. The authors introduce an information-theoretically appropriate measure of its performance, connecting simplification directly to information loss.

Applied to vertebrate retinal responses to 100-millisecond natural movies, the framework finds negligible information loss in the studied ganglion-cell populations even when decoding ignores all correlations. This finding concerns those recordings and stimuli. The analysis also identifies a consequential assumption: treating responses to changing stimuli as stationary over long periods can create apparent correlations that seem to carry substantial information.
neurips-2008-a-general-framework-for-inv.tldr: A framework measures information lost by simplifying neural decoders and finds negligible loss from ignoring correlations in the studied retinal populations.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning involves an optimization problem with a convex-concave structure. The paper targets the computational cost of solving it, focusing on two existing approaches: subgradient descent and semi-infinite linear programming. Both are useful for large problems, but the authors identify different weaknesses in how they construct and update candidate solutions.

Subgradient descent uses the gradient at the current solution without exploiting the full collection of earlier gradients. Semi-infinite linear programming builds a cutting-plane approximation but does not regularize the approximate solution it produces. The proposed method extends a level method for nonsmooth optimization to address both issues within the convex-concave setting.

The algorithm retains information from previously computed gradients and regularizes its solution through projection onto a level set. On eight UCI datasets, it saves an average of 91.9% of computational time relative to semi-infinite linear programming and 70.3% relative to subgradient descent. These are empirical efficiency gains on the evaluated datasets, supporting the value of combining accumulated gradient information with controlled solution updates.
neurips-2008-an-extended-level-method-fo.tldr: An extended level method accelerates multiple kernel learning by reusing past gradients and regularizing updates through level-set projection.

paragraphs: Odor sensors respond slowly and are vulnerable to noise, so their raw readings can be unreliable indicators of an odor's identity. The paper takes inspiration from insect olfaction, where the antennal lobe transforms receptor responses into patterns distributed across neurons and time before a subsequent structure classifies them.

The authors build two connected models. The first is a rate model of the antennal lobe based on integration and inhibition, providing a stage for conditioning sensor signals. The second resembles the sparse, random organization of insect mushroom bodies and serves as the classifier. Its connections adapt through a local Hebbian learning procedure.

The combined system is evaluated on recordings from metal-oxide gas sensors, with the task of distinguishing mixtures from pure odors. It enables fast and accurate discrimination even for highly imbalanced mixtures. The result supports the usefulness of this biological processing sequence for the tested artificial sensing problem, while the models also offer an account of how insect-inspired signal conditioning and classification can work together.
neurips-2008-artificial-olfactory-brain-.tldr: An insect-inspired signal processor and sparse classifier distinguish odor mixtures from pure odors quickly and accurately in gas-sensor recordings.

paragraphs: Kernel regression can benefit from adapting individual kernels when data density, surface curvature, or output noise varies across the input space. However, giving every kernel adjustable parameters creates both computational expense and a risk of overfitting. The paper addresses this tension through a Bayesian formulation of local kernel shaping.

Variational approximations yield an algorithm resembling expectation maximization that estimates regression and kernel parameters together. The authors describe it as computationally efficient for large datasets, requiring no sampling and only one specified prior. It also automatically rejects outliers. The framework applies to regression with local polynomials and provides a way to construct nonstationary Gaussian process regression.

The control motivation is that adaptive controllers and reinforcement learning need reliable estimates of local tangent planes: approximations to how a learned response changes nearby. Spatially adaptive kernels are intended to support those estimates. The authors evaluate the methods on synthetic datasets and on a real robot learning a task-level control law, connecting the regression formulation to an actual control application.
neurips-2008-bayesian-kernel-shaping-for.tldr: A Bayesian algorithm jointly adapts regression models and local kernels, supporting efficient, outlier-resistant estimation for learning control.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between strong rationality assumptions in classical game theory and behavior observed in human economic games. It investigates a model in which reasoning about other players has finite depth and preferences can include more than personal gain. These ingredients provide alternative explanations for how people act in repeated interactions.

The authors place those ingredients inside a partially observable Markov decision process that incorporates interactive reasoning from game theory. The resulting generative model describes how behavior can arise over multiple rounds of an investment game. It captures a broad class of characteristic behaviors, allowing the same framework to express different patterns of interaction.

The authors then reverse the direction of inference: instead of generating actions from a model, they use observed play to classify participants through a recognition model. They apply this procedure to 200 people playing an Investor-Trustee game against randomly matched opponents. The contribution links a behavioral account of limited reasoning and social preferences with a method for recognizing differences among players.
neurips-2008-bayesian-model-of-behaviour.tldr: A Bayesian model combines finite-depth reasoning and non-selfish preferences to explain and classify behavior in repeated economic games.

paragraphs: Understanding a population of neurons requires describing both individual responses and how those responses depend on one another. Single-neuron spike counts are often approximately Poisson distributed, while the joint activity of several neurons can exhibit strong dependence. The paper proposes Poisson copula models to represent these two properties together.

A copula separates the specification of individual response distributions from the structure linking them. This allows the model to retain Poisson distributions for individual spike counts while varying the kind of dependence between neurons. Different copulas describe different patterns of joint activity, providing more detail than a single correlation coefficient.

The authors explore several such models and derive an efficient maximum-likelihood procedure for estimating them from observations. They apply the approach to neuronal recordings, including macaque motor cortex, and quantify the improvement in coding accuracy obtained by incorporating dependencies between pairs of neurons. The contribution is therefore both representational and practical: a richer description of joint responses comes with an estimation method and a measured connection to coding accuracy.
neurips-2008-characterizing-neural-depen.tldr: Poisson copula models capture individual spike-count distributions and richer neural dependencies, whose inclusion improves coding accuracy in the analyzed recordings.

paragraphs: Estimating covariance becomes difficult when vectors have many coordinates but only a limited number of observations are available. The paper addresses this problem by restricting the structure of the covariance estimate. Its eigendecomposition must be representable through a sparse matrix transform, giving the estimation procedure a constrained family of possible solutions.

The transform is assembled from Givens rotations, each of which rotates a pair of coordinates. A greedy likelihood-based procedure estimates the covariance within this framework, while cross-validation selects the number of rotations. This makes the amount of transform structure a choice informed by data, rather than requiring unrestricted estimation of the full covariance.

The authors state that the resulting estimate remains positive definite and well-conditioned even with limited samples. In experiments on hyperspectral data, it consistently produces better covariance estimates than traditional shrinkage estimators across the evaluated classes and sample sizes. These findings support the usefulness of the transform constraint in that setting, combining stable estimates with an efficiently adjustable representation.
neurips-2008-covariance-estimation-for-h.tldr: Constraining covariance through a sparse sequence of coordinate rotations yields stable estimates and improves on shrinkage estimators in hyperspectral experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks directions that explain variation while using a limited number of variables. A common procedure alternates between finding one such direction and modifying the matrix before searching for another. This second operation, called deflation, determines what information remains available to subsequent components.

The paper argues that deflation procedures borrowed from ordinary PCA are seldom appropriate in the sparse setting. This matters because solving the first-component problem carefully does not by itself ensure that later components capture useful additional variation. The authors first develop several heuristic alternatives whose properties better suit the sparse problem.

They then reformulate the optimization objective so that each round explicitly targets the maximum additional variance it can explain. This leads to a generalized deflation procedure, connecting the matrix update to the purpose of extracting another component. On real-world datasets, it typically outperforms more standard techniques. The result emphasizes that constructing a sequence of sparse components requires attention to their cumulative contribution, as well as to each component individually.
neurips-2008-deflation-methods-for-spars.tldr: A generalized deflation procedure makes successive sparse PCA components target additional explained variance and typically improves on standard techniques.

paragraphs: The paper develops exact inference algorithms for binary undirected graphical models under a planarity requirement. These models describe interacting variables with two possible states. The algorithms compute lowest-energy configurations, partition functions, and marginal probabilities, covering both the search for a best configuration and calculations about the model's probability distribution.

The approach uses a correspondence between the graphical model and perfect matchings in an expanded dual graph. This transformation leads to polynomial-time algorithms. Its structural requirement differs from the submodularity constraints used in the graph-cut paradigm: the method does not impose those constraints, but relies on planarity to establish the matching correspondence.

The algorithms also identify worst margin violators, configurations needed for maximum-margin parameter estimation. The authors use that learning procedure in a boundary detection task and report that the approach is efficient and effective. The contribution connects an exact combinatorial inference method to parameter learning, showing how the same planar structure can support several computations required to train and use the model.
neurips-2008-efficient-exact-inference-i.tldr: A perfect-matching formulation enables polynomial-time exact inference for planar binary graphical models without imposing submodularity constraints.

paragraphs: The paper studies approximate maximum a posteriori inference in discrete random fields with pairwise interactions forming a truncated convex model. The task is to find a configuration with low Gibbs energy. The authors propose a move-making algorithm, which improves a candidate configuration through moves computed using source-to-sink minimum cuts.

Its main theoretical advantage is a guarantee on solution quality matching that of the standard linear programming relaxation. Earlier move-making methods offered either weaker bounds or no bound. Compared with approaches that solve the relaxation using interior-point methods or tree-reweighted message passing, the proposed design is faster because it relies only on efficient minimum-cut computations.

The method also directly returns a primal solution, meaning a configuration for the original problem, rather than focusing on the relaxation's dual. Experiments on synthetic and standard real-data problems demonstrate its effectiveness. The analysis raises a further question about connections between move-making methods and randomized rounding of convex relaxations; the authors suggest that exploring this relationship could help develop efficient methods for more complex relaxations.
neurips-2008-improved-moves-for-truncate.tldr: A minimum-cut move-making algorithm matches standard LP-relaxation quality guarantees while providing faster inference and a direct configuration.

paragraphs: Matching objects across two collections usually requires a way to score the similarity of an object in one collection to an object in the other. The paper changes that requirement. Its approach needs similarity measures only within each collection, allowing the matching problem to be expressed through the structure of the two sets.

The proposed criterion chooses pairings that maximize statistical dependence between the matched observations. It measures that dependence using the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. In this formulation, within-collection similarities provide the information used to evaluate an arrangement of pairs, so a direct similarity measure across the two object classes is unnecessary.

The resulting optimization is a quadratic assignment problem with special structure. The authors present a simple algorithm that finds a locally optimal solution. That qualification matters: the stated result concerns local optimality, rather than a guarantee of the best possible assignment. The contribution is a different formulation of object matching, together with a practical optimization procedure for using within-set similarities to construct cross-set correspondences.
neurips-2008-kernelized-sorting-7e20c330.tldr: Kernelized sorting matches objects using only within-set similarities by seeking a locally optimal pairing that maximizes statistical dependence.

paragraphs: Regularized least squares can control overfitting and express a learned function as a kernel expansion. The authors nevertheless identify an interpretive problem, including for constant functions: fitting observations well does not necessarily make the learned function consistent with the kernel. They propose treating consistency with both the data and the kernel as a learning objective.

The new scheme comes with a corresponding representer theorem and an interpretation of which kinds of functions should remain unpenalized. This connects the regularization rule to the behavior the method intends to preserve. The emphasis is therefore on the relationship between a kernel, its associated learning function, and the penalty used during fitting.

Experiments show promising accuracy improvements, while a detailed treatment of heat kernels demonstrates how to apply the approach in a concrete case. The authors present that treatment as a guide for adapting similar techniques to other kernels. They describe the work as a preliminary step toward understanding how function-kernel consistency varies under different distributions, rather than as a completed general account.
neurips-2008-learning-with-consistency-b.tldr: A kernel learning scheme aligns fitted functions with both observations and kernel structure, clarifying penalties and showing promising accuracy gains.

paragraphs: Many datasets record relationships between pairs of objects, such as interactions between proteins or connections between people. Modeling these observations requires care because the simple exchangeability assumptions used by many standard models do not carry over straightforwardly. The paper introduces a family of latent-variable models designed specifically for this relational setting.

Mixed Membership Stochastic Blockmodels extend blockmodels by allowing mixed membership in hidden relational groups. An object can therefore have a representation involving several groups rather than a single exclusive assignment. The resulting object-specific representation is low dimensional and describes latent structure through which the observed relationships can be understood.

The authors develop a general variational algorithm for fast approximate posterior inference. Its role is to infer the hidden relational structure from observed pairwise measurements without requiring exact posterior calculations. Applications to social networks and protein interaction networks explore the model in two different domains. The contribution combines a more flexible account of group membership with an inference procedure that makes the model usable for relational data.
neurips-2008-mixed-membership-stochastic.tldr: Mixed Membership Stochastic Blockmodels represent objects through overlapping latent relational groups and provide fast approximate inference for network data.

paragraphs: Some nonlinear sequences can be represented by switching among modes whose dynamics are conditionally linear. This lets a model describe changing behavior through several simpler dynamical regimes. The paper considers both switching linear dynamical systems and switching vector autoregressive processes, focusing on how to learn persistent, smooth modes when their number is unknown.

The authors use a hierarchical Dirichlet process prior to provide a nonparametric Bayesian approach to that learning problem. Rather than treating the number of modes as known in advance, the framework incorporates uncertainty about the collection of modes. The goal is to discover the dynamical regimes together with the sequence of switches among them.

For inference, the paper develops a sampling algorithm combining a truncated approximation to the Dirichlet process with efficient joint sampling of mode and state sequences. The authors demonstrate utility and flexibility on synthetic data, dancing honey bee sequences, and the IBOVESPA stock index. These applications illustrate the framework across different kinds of temporal observations, with the shared task of learning switching dynamical structure.
neurips-2008-nonparametric-bayesian-lear.tldr: A hierarchical Dirichlet process framework learns an unknown number of persistent dynamical modes in switching linear time-series models.

paragraphs: Regularization provides a common way to understand kernel-based supervised learning. A penalty on a fitted function can also be interpreted through a Bayesian prior, connecting regularized solutions to maximum a posteriori estimation. The paper uses this relationship to investigate a Bayesian account of sparsity in kernel methods.

The proposed construction mixes a point-mass distribution with a distribution the authors call Silverman's g-prior. The point-mass component provides a way to express exact sparsity within the prior formulation. This turns sparsity into a model-choice question handled by Bayesian inference, connecting the selection of a sparse representation to assumptions encoded in the prior.

The paper's main contribution is theoretical: it analyzes posterior consistency for the resulting Bayesian model-choice procedure. This concerns the procedure's behavior as evidence accumulates, rather than simply its fit to a fixed dataset. The authors also establish an asymptotic relationship with the Bayesian information criterion. Together, these results connect the proposed sparse Bayesian formulation to both large-sample model-choice behavior and an established criterion for comparing models.
neurips-2008-posterior-consistency-of-th.tldr: The paper analyzes posterior consistency and the asymptotic connection to BIC for sparse Bayesian kernel model choice using Silverman's g-prior.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a useful logistic regression classifier from private data while protecting the database. Its first approach measures the sensitivity of logistic regression, meaning how much the learned result can change when the underlying data changes. It then adds noise to the fitted classifier in proportion to that sensitivity.

The authors identify limitations in extending this strategy to other learning algorithms and introduce a second approach for logistic regression. This method perturbs the optimization objective itself and solves the modified problem. It therefore places the privacy mechanism inside the learning procedure and does not depend on the sensitivity calculation used by the first method.

For the proposed objective-based algorithm, the paper proves privacy in the stated Dwork framework and supplies a learning-performance guarantee. These results address both sides of the motivating tradeoff: protecting data and retaining the ability to learn. The work also identifies a connection between regularization and privacy, linking a familiar tool for controlling learning behavior to the construction of private algorithms.
neurips-2008-privacy-preserving-logistic.tldr: Private logistic regression can be learned by perturbing its objective, with formal privacy and learning guarantees and a connection to regularization.

paragraphs: Support vector machines classify by maximizing the margin separating two classes. The paper identifies a sensitivity in this objective: directions along which the data have a large spread can dominate the solution. As a result, the separation can be biased toward cutting along those directions, tying the chosen boundary strongly to the geometry of data variation.

The authors propose maximizing a margin measured relative to the spread of the data. This changes how candidate separating boundaries are judged. A separation is evaluated in relation to the variation present in the data, so the formulation directly addresses the influence that large-spread directions have on the ordinary margin objective.

The proposed optimization can be solved efficiently, making the change in objective computationally usable. Experiments on digit datasets show drastic performance improvements over support vector machines. Those findings support the relative-margin formulation in the evaluated classification problems. The broader methodological contribution is to make data spread part of the margin criterion itself, rather than leaving its influence implicit in the geometry of the solution.
neurips-2008-relative-margin-machines-c6.tldr: Relative Margin Machines measure separation against data spread and show drastic improvements over SVMs on digit datasets.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many noisy measurements are needed to identify which entries of a high-dimensional sparse vector are nonzero. The unknown vector has n coordinates, of which k are active, and is observed through m random measurements. The goal is reliable recovery of the active pattern, connecting sparse coding to a precise statistical detection problem.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions involving the dimensions and signal-to-noise ratio. Their necessary condition says that, at a given signal-to-noise ratio, perfect recovery requires measurements scaling at least as k times log(n−k). This restriction applies to all algorithms, regardless of computational complexity, and strengthens previous necessary conditions.

They also show that this measurement scaling is sufficient for a simple maximum-correlation estimator to succeed under their analysis. The matching scaling establishes optimality at that level without requiring more sophisticated sparse-recovery methods. Because the sufficient estimator is simple, the authors argue that achieving the optimal scaling can be biologically plausible. The reliability statements are asymptotic, concerning behavior as problem dimensions grow.
neurips-2008-resolution-limits-of-sparse.tldr: The paper establishes an optimal measurement scaling for sparse-pattern recovery and shows that a simple maximum-correlation estimator can achieve it.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis extends PCA to nonlinear feature extraction by representing observations in a feature space where linear modeling is possible. A kernel makes this representation implicit, so the method can operate without directly constructing the feature coordinates. However, that implicit representation also makes some extensions of ordinary PCA difficult to transfer.

The paper tackles this obstacle for robust inference. It introduces a new cost function for performing inference in kernel PCA and uses it to build a unified treatment of noise, missing data, and outliers. The contribution addresses how to work with imperfect observations when the space in which PCA operates is available only through a kernel.

Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that the resulting algorithm outperforms existing methods in the reported evaluations. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed inference formulation across the tested settings. More broadly, the work supplies a route for bringing robust treatment of observations into nonlinear PCA, while retaining the implicit feature-space representation that defines the kernel approach.
neurips-2008-robust-kernel-principal-com.tldr: A new inference cost function extends kernel PCA to jointly address noise, missing observations, and outliers.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object's category does not necessarily reveal its pose or the locations of its particular regions. The paper develops LOOPS to provide this more detailed description. Trained for an object class, the method learns a model combining shape and image features and uses it to outline new instances in images.

A notable feature is the relationship between its training annotations and learned representation. Training provides outlines without correspondences across instances, yet the model develops landmark points that recur consistently across objects. These landmarks can be accurately localized in an image, giving the resulting outline an internal structure useful for comparing instances.

The authors report state-of-the-art outlining results for objects with large deformations and articulations in cluttered natural images. This supports the model's ability to handle substantial shape variation in the evaluated setting. The resulting localizations can support descriptive classification, search, and clustering: tasks that benefit from knowing how an object is arranged and where its regions lie, in addition to knowing its class.
neurips-2008-shape-based-object-localiza.tldr: LOOPS learns consistent landmarks from uncorresponded outlines and precisely localizes deformable objects in cluttered images.

paragraphs: The paper combines two tasks: dividing images into regions and discovering object categories shared across an image collection. Its framework is unsupervised, so the categories are learned as part of the process. The statistical design is motivated by an analysis of manually segmented scenes, where chi-square tests support power-law distributions for object frequencies and segment sizes.

A Pitman-Yor process provides a prior suited to those observed distributions. It allows the learning procedure to discover an unknown collection of objects and lets segmentation resolution adapt to individual images. The authors also incorporate Gaussian processes to obtain spatially contiguous regions that respect image boundaries, connecting category discovery with the spatial organization of scenes.

Inference uses a new family of variational approximations. The resulting segmentations compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods while the model simultaneously discovers categories shared across natural scenes. The contribution is this combination: a distributional account of how often objects occur and how large segments are, coupled with spatial modeling and joint discovery across a database.
neurips-2008-shared-segmentation-of-natu.tldr: A Pitman-Yor-based model jointly segments natural images and discovers shared object categories while adapting region resolution to each image.

paragraphs: Policy gradient algorithms have strong local convergence guarantees, but noisy gradient estimates can limit learning performance. The paper studies this problem through a signal-to-noise ratio for policy updates, examining the Weight Perturbation algorithm in detail. It finds that this measure predicts long-term learning performance and that cost-to-go is the optimal baseline within its episodic formulation.

The authors then change the sampling distributions used for perturbations to improve that ratio. One modification uses anisotropic sampling, allowing perturbations to vary by direction. This introduces bias into the update while increasing signal-to-noise ratio; the authors interpret the bias as following the natural gradient of the cost function.

A second modification uses non-Gaussian sampling. The paper shows that such distributions can improve signal-to-noise ratio and argues that the best isotropic choice is a shell distribution, with constant perturbation magnitude and uniformly distributed direction. Both modifications produce substantial learning improvements in the reported challenging experiments. The findings make perturbation geometry a concrete design choice for improving policy gradient learning.
neurips-2008-signal-to-noise-ratio-analy.tldr: Signal-to-noise analysis motivates directional and non-Gaussian perturbations that substantially improve policy gradient learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to identify useful skills from the structure of an agent's interaction with its environment. It represents that interaction as a graph and characterizes a useful class of skills through betweenness, a graph-centrality measure. This ties the choice of skills to structural properties of the environment's interaction graph.

The characterization can be used directly to form a set of skills suitable for a particular environment. In that use, the graph-based criterion supplies a principled basis for selecting skills. The contribution is a description of what makes this class useful, providing a target for skill construction rather than treating the skill set as an arbitrary input.

The authors emphasize a second role: guiding online, incremental skill-discovery algorithms. Such algorithms need not know or represent the complete environment graph. This matters because the characterization can inform discovery as interaction unfolds, even when a full graph is unavailable. The stated contribution is a structural guide for developing these methods, alongside its direct use in forming environment-specific skills.
neurips-2008-skill-characterization-base.tldr: Graph betweenness characterizes a useful class of skills and guides incremental discovery without requiring the complete environment graph.

paragraphs: Online learning updates a model as observations arrive, but the resulting weight vector need not be sparse. The paper introduces truncated gradient, a general method for encouraging zero weights in online algorithms with convex loss. This makes sparsity part of the ongoing update process rather than requiring a separate batch-fitting procedure.

A parameter controls the rate of sparsification continuously, ranging from no sparsification to total sparsification. The method also has a theoretical connection to a familiar batch approach: one instance can be understood as an online counterpart of L1 regularization. This gives the update rule an interpretation grounded in regularized learning.

The authors prove that small sparsification rates add only a small amount of regret relative to typical online-learning guarantees. This provides a qualified statement about the cost of encouraging sparsity, rather than claiming it is always free. Experiments on several datasets find substantial discoverable sparsity when the number of features is large, supporting the method's practical usefulness for producing sparse models during online learning.
neurips-2008-sparse-online-learning-via-.tldr: Truncated gradient induces adjustable sparsity in online learning, with small additional regret at small sparsification rates.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian model for documents that already have parse trees. Its purpose is to combine thematic information with grammatical structure. Topic models supply a way to represent what a document discusses, while parse trees provide relationships that constrain how its words fit together syntactically.

In the proposed model, each word is generated from a distribution combining document-specific topic weights with syntactic transitions associated with the parse tree. Word generation follows an order consistent with that tree. The model therefore makes both document context and syntactic relationships part of the same account of how words arise.

The authors derive approximate posterior inference using variational methods for hierarchical Dirichlet processes. This supplies a way to infer the model's hidden structure from parsed observations. They report qualitative and quantitative results on synthetic data and hand-parsed documents. The contribution is the joint formulation and its inference method, with those evaluations examining a model in which thematic and syntactic constraints act together at the level of individual words.
neurips-2008-syntactic-topic-models-7000.tldr: Syntactic Topic Models combine document topics and parse-tree transitions in a Bayesian account of word generation.
